cards.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's letter to staff about affair

depth.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's **letter to staff** about an **affair** has commenters debating whether he should face consequences

Some commenters think the board may **keep him** because of his value to Nvidia; others object to **excusing his conduct**. The **spy allegations** are disputed too, with commenters questioning whether they are true.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the affair should bring consequences; others think the board may keep him because of his value to Nvidia.

comments.text: Spooks from CIA must be aware of this for a long time. The only question now is why this information is leaked now? What is the distraction they are trying to create by leaking this now?

Take this with a grain of salt, but my guess is that the board on some level has to judge him as being so high performing that they would try to keep him as long as that doesn't cause too much PR damage to the company, or the deals get them in too much trouble with the government. This is just a total guess, but I assume what a lot of the board want is for him to sell as much to China or indirect…

I heard a guy I respect say “there’s a short list of things people will ruin their lives for.” I’m not sure if this will ruin Jensen’s life or not, but it’s a good opportunity for us all to remember that the short-term high is usually not worth it.

Now we have to re-evaluate all his statements in favor of selling to China. For example, we want China to build on "our stack". On the face of it, that seems correct. If China has multiple stacks to pick from why wouldn't we want them to pick our stack? But do they have such a choice?

In parts of Asia it is "expected" that a successful politician or businessman will have a "second family". I'm thinking the spying part (Huang is from Taiwan and was possibly leaking info to China) is considered worse than the cheating part by everyone involved.

cards.title: KetchUp – Open-source SketchUp alternative built with Rust and WebGPU

depth.text: someone built a **free 3D app** for planning **woodworking and furniture projects** before making them

The page calls it **BenchUp**: it runs in a browser or as a desktop app, and saves your work **locally**. It can import **SketchUp geometry** or export OBJ, but SketchUp textures, scenes, and some model features aren’t supported.

cards.camps: Two camps: SketchUp fans are excited by a successor; others say its workflow differs or report glitches.

comments.text: As a very long time user and lover of SketchUp, I'm still peeved about the direction Trimble took in neglecting the SketchUp desktop modeler in favor of a web-based UI. Their licensing was also terrible... first they discontinued the free version of SketchUp, and then later on they discontinued perpetual licensing, meaning the only way to get the desktop modeler was to pay several hundred per…

I had a very high level look at the repo, only 161k lines of code (probably including a bunch of tests and config). Not too bad. And it uses a project called openskp [1] to work with SketchUp files, also AI coded to some extend, but looks reasonable at a glance. [1] - https://github.com/iamahsanmehmood/openskp

This is awesome. At the same time I wonder if we are entering an era in which it’s just better to build your own tools Need a 3D modeler? Use Claude or codex to build the 3D model first, then build the modeler around it as you iterate towards what you want to build So many times I’ve had to spend hours learning a software, reading docs, doing tutorials, only to later be able to do a small basic…

This is so awesome and something I definitely need. I'm a very casual user of SketchUp (I use it once every few months), but I have a single file which is a detailed model of my house, which I have invested many hours in creating, and that only works on the full Desktop app. So the free web app is not an option for me. And a subscription doesn't make financial sense so I have to ask for a new…

To this day I still use the 2017 freeware version (through WINE) for drafting all my home projects. It's just so darned intuitive to me (for anything without too many curves, at least) and I can't be bothered to learn anything else. The web version works in a pinch but it has always felt slower and less capable to me. Going to have to try this!

cards.title: Outlook.com is rejecting email from domains without DMARC

depth.text: Outlook.com is **bouncing** some **small senders’ emails** when their domains lack a key record

Outlook.com began this on **November 5, 2026**, and it can hit even **low-volume senders**; only some messages bounce. The suggested fix is a TXT record, **v=DMARC1; p=none**, which asks receivers to take no action on failures.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say DMARC is overdue and helps reduce spam; critics say Microsoft should not roll it out silently and already mishandles legitimate mail.

comments.text: Outlook.com is also rejecting mail based on blocklists that are not public and you essentialy cannot get yourself out. My VPS provider is pretty much entirely blocked and their regular blocklist process says we are golden so nothing to unblock. Outlook.com and similar are an anathema to email. This is why they tell you not to run a mail server . On the other hand rejecting domains without dmarc…
Sounds like something every mail sender should have done already. Good for Microsoft customers and I don't care one bit for the lazy people who have to late-patch now.

Outlook.com has quietly dropped[0] emails from certain domains/IPs for years, even with SPF/DKIM/DMARC all properly set up and no history of spam. As someone who's administering their own mail server, Outlook has been the bane of my existence. [0]: As in: They accepted the email just fine (according to the logs) but it still didn't end up in the recipient's mailbox.
They're not rejecting them quietly. They're sending 5xx permanent delivery failures.

I set up DMARC on my personal domain so long ago I can't even remember when I did it. 10 years+? I had kinda assumed that a lot of providers would start rejecting domains without DMARC support. I'm surprised it's happening this late.

cards.title: RIP, Harvest

depth.text: Harvest **raised prices sharply** and started answering customer emails with **AI-generated walls of text**

The writer says their monthly bill jumped from **$13.32 to $133.98** after Bending Spoons moved users to a new “enterprise” plan; the cheaper “flex” plan adds **2%** on top of card fees. They say Harvest support now sends replies from a Large Language Model instead of reading customer emails.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the “SaaS is dead” talk is overblown; others say AI clones are making software easier to replace.

comments.text: We recently went through a version of this with Asana when we discovered their "per seat" pricing is sold in groups of 5 seats. Going from 5->6 users adjusts your bill to 5->10 seats, doubling your price. It isn't about the money, the principle is gross. Thankfully Asana's core business is now a prompt. We are nearly done replacing it with a native, self hosted client. Will post about it once it…

It's a shame. They tried to increase our prices about 800%. I actually liked the software and used it for over 15 years across a couple of services businesses. They do have this "usage based pricing" where you pay them for each user, but then also for each project and customer, and then a percentage of your billings. It's completely absurd to be paying them a percentage when you receive payments…

Odoo CE (community edition) is open source and has built in stripe integration (along with a few other payment providers) that will invoice on time spent against projects/tasks. If you’re in a region that has l10n for accounting (via the OCA), you’d be able to handle all your tax compliance also. Only caveat to Odoo CE is you’d need to self host, which in itself is not that difficult…

Used Harvest for many years. Was talking to an agency owner friend of mine who had been using it, but once Bending Spoons jacked up the price they jumped for their own self-cooked version. The "SaaS is dead" narrative is a bit overblown, but private equity needs to think twice before gouging folks these days.
Bending Spoons tried to 2x my Harvest bill on the usage-based plan and 146x (yes, that's not a percentage) on the unlimited plan. I switched to Clockify [1] and it works well. 1: https://clockify.me/

cards.title: Dux: Free, open-source Wayland desktop shell with file manager and theming

depth.text: Dux is a **free desktop shell** with a **file manager**, matching themes, and handy system tools

The DMS 2.1 Stormborn release adds a **system monitor**, **video wallpapers**, and a revamped media player. It also has a keyboard-first file manager with tabs and split view, and generates **matching colors** for supported GTK and Qt apps, terminals, and editors.

cards.camps: Two camps: users praise its polish and reliability; others prefer minimal setups or question its maturity, resource use, and name.

comments.text: Been using this for close to a year (wrote about it here when it was still called Dank Material Shell: https://tedium.co/2026/01/29/niri-danklinux-scrolling-window... ); it is endlessly slick, and I think good enough to help mainstream Niri. It also just added official support for atomic distros like Bazzite; it was previously kind of an annoying gap given the popularity of those distros.

I was confused for a second, but turns out DMS rebranded the 'Dank' to 'Dux' a few weeks ago [1]. I've been running DMS + Niri for nearly a year now with no intentions of switching anytime soon. Given how often I've historically changed shells/DEs, this is the ricing equivalent to settling down, getting married, and having kids. [1] https://duxlabs.dev/blog/v2-0-release

None of them seems to be aware that "Dux" is not really a good word, because it's the name used by Benito Mussolini for himself.
It reads the same as calling this WM "Fuhrer". Not a good name choice.
Average look, from the software part, not mature enough compared to other setups such as hyprland or sway.

This looks at lot like Android. I am not sure how I feel about the curl | sh installation. This seems lile the kind of project which should become part of a Linux distro and thoroughly reviewed before it can be trusted unconditionally.

https://wiki.xfce.org/releng/wayland_roadmap
My most anticipated development roadmap these days.

cards.title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world

depth.text: someone found a way to **unlock cars remotely** using just a **number plate**

The researchers linked a plate to an account, then used **admin credentials embedded in a JavaScript bundle**, a path-traversal trick and an **MFA bypass** to mint an app token and send car commands. They say the combined attack worked on vehicles in **Australia, the United States and Canada**.

cards.camps: Some commenters see connected cars as a security and privacy problem; others say an attack that took weeks and multiple people isn't a big worry for ordinary owners.

comments.text: Blue car in the background is a facelifted fifth gen RAV4. Obvious from the shape of the mirrors and headlight. Toyota/Lexus would align with the "both brands" remark. White one is harder to tell obviously, but the shape of the mirror looks the same, and you can see the top of the dash has a chamfered shape that looks an awful lot like this pic…

These always connected cars will soon become as bad, or likely worse, than the smartphones of today, which we don't really own and control, and always tracked. You will need an online account with obscure terms of service to use the car, won't be able to repair yourself, your data being sold, etc. Evil.
“Any car” is perhaps too strong a claim. If it is Toyota/Lexus, I will say that I don’t think my 2009 Camry has this issue. I am quite sure that the fourth-generation Hilux my brother has does not.
The follow up/linked article at the bottom is worth a read too as it's the 'world-wide' part of it. Definitely a great read from both Sam and Shubs https://samcurry.net/forgerock?ref=shubs.io

cards.title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry

depth.text: someone set up a **task queue** to keep **AI coding work** from **frying their focus**

Tickets are **Markdown files in the repo**, and an agent researches them, builds the ones marked safe, runs tests, and checks the browser. A Claude artifact shows the board for review; the **owner inbox** gathers decisions for the human, and production deployment stays with the author. The author handles **one item at a time**, then puts it back in the queue so its context doesn't keep occupying their memory.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say limit parallel tasks and focus on one thing; others use queues and tools to manage several agent tasks at once.

comments.text: I've learned that rather than juggle too much, I just accept that I'm still more productive than ever before, even if I'm "idle", it's important to take time to have a break and to recharge, refresh and reflect. So I limit myself to at most 2 or 3 things at once, and if all of those are in long running sessions, well so be it, I know I'll be deep back in it soon. But it's tempting to start "just…

Here’s what I do: I sit down for 45 min to 1 hour and write up in English a detailed explanation of what I want. Then I hand it over to my agent to implement. Then I go on to the next task. Really I’m just writing. Not so much prompting. I define prompting as an interactive and often reactive interaction mode with AI. Instead, I just write.

This only solves part of the problem, the other half is: ok so you have 3 chats going, at some point you realize you have 3 >10k line CLs to review, on top of code your colleagues are asking you to review. Every review I’ve ever done I’ve found overfitting and brittle solutions and things tacked on instead of integrated so I refuse to give up on code reviews, but those are my real bottleneck, and…

I feel like I’m starting to have my own psychosis where if I read a blog article and I get a whiff of AI smell my brain turns off and I can’t read anymore. I’m not blaming the author maybe this is their original idea and its edited by AI but I physically can’t keep reading it. AI blindness or something.

I have almost the exact same workflow. With just about everything I do, I create little websites to help me with code review, or multitasking on tickets, or reviewing a spec, or whatever I happen to be doing, any workflow gets turned into a throwaway site that works like a work queue or form. I've had trouble teaching this approach to others. The way I cope with AI Brain Fry is owed to Starcraft…

cards.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists

depth.text: someone thinks the **AI bubble** may not pop, despite all the **money being spent**

The author points to **3 trillion dollars** in commitments and an estimated **1.9 trillion** already spent, arguing data-centre costs are one-off and demand can grow. Anthropic's filing says it makes $2.08 for every $1 of compute, while commenters push back that **hardware wears out** and revenue is not profit.

cards.camps: Two camps: optimists say AI's potential uses and demand can justify the investment; skeptics say recurring hardware costs and competition could squeeze AI labs' profits.

comments.text: Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit. Everybody knew it. But some investors don't have the patience for these "sure things" to mature into their commercial destiny and others know they can siphon off a killing by taking advantage of them as they speculate. These bubbles aren't about potential, they're about…

> Profits Can Grow, By A Lot Profits are mentioned but then only revenue is discussed, Revenue != Profit. Revenue can grow yeah but experimentation/token-maxing stage is ending and price wars have started, so I'm not sure about rising profits, AI Labs won't necessary be able to capture the margin(>>China<<), it might be companies/consumers who will capture most of it, if so there is a bubble - it…

Big red flags that I think point the other way: - anthropic IPO repricing - pareto frontier gap decreasing by the month between open and closed models - SpaceX disappoinment - enterprise buyers as main consumers of closed tokens are being displaced by OS competition for pennies - job loss and entry level hiring collapse - massive discounts of current data center contract debt - consumer open…

Im not convinced by the claims of infrastructure only being expensive to build initially. Hardware doesn't last forever especially in a data center, maintenance isn't free, electricity is not going to get significantly cheaper. If models get more efficient we won't need super expensive and expansive hardware build outs, if models keep getting more powerful and needy and are hardware limited, each…

I dont know if the valuations make sense, but the usability is all there and so are the potential profits. Over a decade, that's probably all that matters. If the valuations pop or dip (anytime soon), I think that's mostly irrelevant. I get that the press probably doesn't like to hear this boring conclusion. P.S: A Matlab/Physics simulation guy running for a Liberal party seat in Canada? Say more!

cards.title: Every processor die anyone has photographed and given away

depth.text: someone collected **free photos** of **processor dies** from the early days of chips to today

The gallery has **357 processors**, photographed from 1971 to 2024. Seeing a die means sanding or dissolving the package away, then photographing what's left through a microscope; 115 chips with known sizes can be compared at **true scale**.

comments.text: I would pay for this as a high quality book. Ideally some info and detail about each processor. Anyone else?

With the early dies with thousands of transistors you really can see the logic gates, once it gets to the millions you can see the structures minimized and multiplied but once it gets to the billions on modern dies it becomes so small and abstract I wonder if any image can capture the detail contained in them.

That maker list is unusable. It's not sorted in any way, contains duplicates (MOS Technology & Commodore CSG are the same), and would gain from reorganizing some brands (gathering Nintendo CPUs together, for instance).
See also Ken Shirriff's blog, which has die photos plus detailed explanation of how things work. https://www.righto.com/ https://news.ycombinator.com/from?site=righto.com
Have people tried training models to decode these photographs into code?

glossary.honey trap: A romantic or sexual setup used to get secrets or pressure someone.
glossary.stack: A pile of values where a program adds items to the top and removes them from there.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.WebGPU: A browser feature that lets a web page run calculations on your device’s graphics chip.
glossary.WebGL2: A browser feature that lets websites draw interactive 3D scenes.
glossary.Push/Pull: A tool that turns a flat drawn shape into a thicker 3D form.
glossary.Wavefront OBJ: A file type for saving 3D shapes so another app can open them.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.DMARC: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: rules for checking whether email claiming to come from a domain is genuine.
glossary.SPF: Sender Policy Framework: a way for a domain to say which mail servers are allowed to send email for it.
glossary.DKIM: DomainKeys Identified Mail: a way for an email to carry proof about who sent it.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.TXT record: A kind of domain setting that stores text, such as email instructions.
glossary.5xx delivery failure: A mail-server error that says an email was rejected, rather than just delayed.
glossary.Large Language Model: A kind of AI that can write text in response to what you ask it.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.ACH: Automated Clearing House: a US system banks use to send money between accounts electronically.
glossary.chargeback: A payment reversal requested through a card provider, often when someone disputes a charge.
glossary.usage-based pricing: A bill that changes based on how much or what parts of a service you use.
glossary.desktop shell: The part of a desktop that provides things like panels, menus, and everyday controls.
glossary.Wayland: A system Linux desktops use to draw windows and handle mouse and keyboard input.
glossary.compositor: The part of a desktop that puts app windows together and manages how they appear on screen.
glossary.immutable OS: An operating system whose core parts are kept unchanged during normal use.
glossary.GTK: GIMP Toolkit: a set of ready-made parts for building desktop app windows and controls.
glossary.Qt: A set of tools developers use to build app windows and controls.
glossary.QML: Qt Modeling Language: a language developers use to lay out app screens and describe how they behave.
glossary.VIN: Vehicle Identification Number: a number that identifies a particular vehicle.
glossary.APK: The file you download to install an Android app.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.OpenIDM: Identity software the automaker used to manage accounts on its connected-car platform.
glossary.path traversal: A trick that uses a specially written file path to reach files a program was meant to keep off-limits.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall: a website’s guard that checks incoming requests and can block suspicious ones.
glossary.MFA: Multi-factor authentication: a login check that asks for more than one kind of proof.
glossary.ROPC: Resource Owner Password Credentials: a login method where an app sends a user's password to get a sign-in token.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.git: A tool that keeps a history of changes to code or other files.
glossary.priority queue: A list that puts the most important waiting task first.
glossary.Markdown: A plain-text way to format notes with headings, lists, and code.
glossary.branch: A separate line of code changes where you can work without changing the main version straight away.
glossary.production: The live version of software that people are actually using.
glossary.Claude artifact: A page Claude can create to display information or tools; here it shows the work board.
glossary.ROAS: Return on ad spend: a way to compare money earned from ads with the money spent on them.
glossary.RSS reader: An app that gathers updates from websites and shows them in one place.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.AI bubble: A worry that excitement about AI has pushed company prices too high, and they could fall if the businesses do not make enough money.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.data centre: A building full of computers that companies use to run online services.
glossary.moat: An advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take customers away from a business.
glossary.P/E ratio: Price-to-earnings ratio: a comparison between what a company's shares cost and how much money it earns.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.S-1 filing: A document a company gives US regulators when it plans to sell shares to the public.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.convertible notes: Loans that can later turn into company shares.
glossary.false vocal folds: Tissue above the vocal folds that can help make some throat-singing sounds.
glossary.overtone: A higher sound that can be heard alongside a lower sound.
glossary.processor die: The flat piece inside a processor package where the processor's parts are made.
glossary.transistor: A tiny electronic switch that helps control the flow of electricity inside a computer.
glossary.logic gate: A small part of a chip that combines yes-or-no signals to do simple calculations.
